claims.text: Annealing cold-worked HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 0.4–0.5 Tm for less than 10 minutes in an inert atmosphere will induce partial recrystallization.
Partial recrystallization of HfZrTiTa0.53 will produce a heterogeneous mixture of nanoscale, ultrafine, and moderate-sized grains.
The annealed HfZrTiTa0.53 microstructure will retain nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries.
The heterogeneous grain structure will improve tensile ductility and delay loss of uniform deformation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Uniform tensile elongation will increase from approximately 13.5% to approximately 20%.
The annealed alloy will retain a yield strength of approximately 780–800 MPa.
The annealed alloy will retain a compressive strength near 1300 MPa.
The annealed alloy will preserve impact-triggered energy release comparable to the untreated baseline.
As-cold-worked HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-cold-worked HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% strain for HfZrTiTa0.53 is a uniform tensile elongation.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has established impact-triggered energetic performance.
Partial-recrystallization annealing will relieve residual internal stresses.
Partial recrystallization will dissipate locally concentrated dislocation structures in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Locally concentrated dislocation structures are responsible for early tensile necking in the untreated alloy.
Retained nanoscale microstructural features will reinforce the alloy's high strength after annealing.
Retained nanoscale microstructural features will preserve the alloy's energetic response.
The proposed short anneal will avoid detrimental coarsening of strengthening phases.

The tensile and compression predictions are scoped to room-to-moderate temperatures and quasi-static strain rates near 10^-3 s^-1, while impact testing is intended to reproduce prior impact conditions.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary distinguish quasi-static tension/compression from prior-like impact testing, but the experiment design can be read as assigning the same approximately 10^-3 s^-1 strain rate to tensile, compression, and impact tests. A genuine impact test cannot simultaneously use that quasi-static rate.
These fields recast the reported 13.5% terminal strain as uniform tensile elongation, although the task context does not identify it as a tensile uniform-elongation baseline.
